newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu readies peace steps ahead of U.S. trip.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu readies peace steps ahead of U.S. trip.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu prepared for a trip to the United States this week by setting up the next peace steps with the Palestinians and slapping down a burgeoning debate over Israel's occupation of a strip of Lebanon.
Netanyahu's office said a special cabinet meeting would be held on Monday ahead of his talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday.

Netanyahu told a joint news conference with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat at Erez on the Gaza Strip border that they had agreed to start detailed talks on further peace moves in their Hebron accord.

"We agreed on a mechanism to resolve these issues and advance them," he said, adding that Israeli-Palestinian committees would begin talks next Sunday with a committee on economics meeting before that.
Israel handed 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule in January after months of acrimonious wrangling over a deal undertaken by Israel's previous government.

The Hebron handover calmed Arab fears that Netanyahu, who won elections last May, might not continue the peace process. U.S. officials said the accord should be used as a springboard for a renewal of peace talks with Syria.

Since the handover, Arafat has complained of delays on other issues in the Hebron deal, including the operation of Palestinian sea and air ports, the release of Palestinian prisoners and "free passage" between Gaza and the West Bank.

But he struck an optimistic note on Sunday, saying: "We had a very important meeting...We discussed the details of the problems we are facing, especially the points which have to be implemented after the Hebron agreement."
Palestinian officials said Arafat would go to Hebron on Monday and Israel Radio said he might receive Palestinian women prisoners being freed by Israel.

Before meeting Arafat, Netanyahu, in a statement to the media, called for an end to a public debate on a unilateral Israeli troop pullout from south Lebanon, saying such talk could encourage attacks on Israeli soldiers.

He made the appeal after seven Israeli soldiers were wounded in a clash with guerrillas in Israel's occupation zone, carved out in 1985. On Tuesday, 73 troops were killed in a collision of two helicopters heading there.

Netanyahu said: "We are not in Lebanon to rule it but to ensure security for Israel's northern settlements. As long as this aim obliges us to remain in Lebanon, that is the way we will continue to act."
